summary:
MARS PATHFINDER is a route planner in the browser for astronauts walking on Mars. You pick a start point and an end point on real HiRISE terrain from Jezero Crater, and it finds a route a suited astronaut could actually walk. It's a static React, TypeScript, and Vite app with no backend, and it's hosted on GitHub Pages.

The terrain is a HiRISE elevation model turned into a grid of cells about 0.95m by 1m. Each cell stores its slope (Horn's method), its roughness (the bumpiness left after fitting a flat plane), and a flag for data quality.

Routing uses A* search, moving in eight directions across the grid. Each step costs its length, increased for slope, roughness, s,s and uncertain data. Any step with a grade over 20° is ruled out. There are three route modes: shortest, terrain-aware, and uncertainty-aware. Every step costs at least its own length, and the search aims by straight-line distance, so A* always finds the best route on the grid. Ties are broken the same way every time, so the same inputs always give the same route.

The app draws each route on a 2D map and in a 3D view. It shows distance, total climb and descent, peak slope and grade, and how much of the route crosses uncertain ground. A search visualiser compares A*, Dijkstra, and greedy search side by side.

The project has 281 unit tests, 40 simulation cases and 21 browser tests, and they all run on every push. On real Jezero terrain, routes come out 7 to 9% longer than a straight line and take 50 to 220 ms.
details:
What it does and how it works

MARS PATHFINDER plans walking routes for astronauts on Mars. You pick a start and an end point on real terrain from Jezero Crater, where NASA's Perseverance rover landed, and the app finds a route a person in a spacesuit could actually walk. We took a HiRISE elevation model and turned it into a grid of cells about 1 metre across. Each cell stores its slope, ground roughness, and data reliability. An A* search then looks for the cheapest path across that grid. Each step costs its length, with extra cost for steep, rough, or uncertain ground, and any step steeper than 20° is ruled out. Users can choose between three route modes: shortest, terrain-aware,e and uncertainty-aware. They can see the route on a 2D map and in a 3D view, along with its distance, climb, steepest point,nt and how much of it crosses uncertain ground.

Benefits and intended impact

Astronauts on foot move slowly, carry limited oxygen, and face real fall risks. A route that's 8% longer but avoids a steep slope can be the safer choice. Our tool makes that trade-off visible and easy to measure, so mission planners and students can test routes before anyone sets foot on the ground. We built it as a learning tool too: a built-in visualiser shows how A*, Dijkstra, and greedy search explore the map differently, which makes pathfinding easier to understand.

Tools and technologies

TypeScript and React 19, built with Vite. Three.js for the 3D terrain. Python for processing the terrain data from HiRISE and CTX. Vitest for unit tests and Playwright for browser tests. GitHub Actions for automated testing and deployment to GitHub Pages. No special hardware is needed, and the whole thing runs in the browser with no server.

Creativity

Most route planners work on road maps. Ours works on raw elevation data from another planet. It also treats uncertainty in the data as part of the cost, not as an afterthought. We also corrected for the way the Mars map projection stretches distances, so lengths are measured in true ground metres.

Factors we considered

- Astronaut safety: limits on slope and grade.

- Honesty about data quality: we flag terrain we can't trust.

- Reproducibility: the same inputs always give the same route.

- Performance: routes take 50 to 220 ms in the browser.

- Correctness: 281 unit tests, 40 simulation scenarios,s and 21 browser tests run on every change.

- Credit: We credit and license all NASA and USGS data properly.
